questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to design a memory pool that balances locality, contention, and simplicity for low-latency code.

## Key Concepts
- Thread-local caches to reduce lock contention
- Global pool synchronization (lock-free vs. lock-backed)
- Fixed-size blocks using free lists
- Fragmentation and worst-case latency considerations

## Data Structures
```c
typedef struct Block { struct Block* next; } Block;

typedef struct {
    Block* local_cache;
    Block* global_head;
    size_t local_count;
    size_t local_capacity;
    pthread_mutex_t global_lock;
} Allocator;
```

## API
```c
void  init_allocator(Allocator* a, Block* pool, size_t n);
void* allocate(Allocator* a);
void  free(Allocator* a, void* ptr);
void  destroy_allocator(Allocator* a);
```

## Synchronization Strategy
**Lock-backed approach** (simpler, sufficient for most cases):
- Use a single mutex protecting the global free list
- Per-thread caches are lock-free (each thread has exclusive access)
- Global lock only acquired during cache refill/drain operations

**Lock-free alternative**:
- Use atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) on the global head pointer
- Higher complexity but eliminates global lock contention entirely
- Suitable for extremely high contention scenarios

## Pseudo-code

### allocate()
```
function allocate(a):
    if a.local_cache not empty:
        block = pop(a.local_cache)
        a.local_count--
        return block
    
    lock(a.global_lock)
    while a.local_count < CACHE_SIZE and a.global_head not null:
        block = pop(a.global_head)
        push(a.local_cache, block)
        a.local_count++
    unlock(a.global_lock)
    
    if a.local_cache not empty:
        block = pop(a.local_cache)
        a.local_count--
        return block
    
    return NULL  // out of memory
```

### free()
```
function free(a, block):
    push(a.local_cache, block)
    a.local_count++
    
    if a.local_count >= CACHE_SIZE:
        lock(a.global_lock)
        for i = 0 to CACHE_SIZE/2:
            block = pop(a.local_cache)
            push(a.global_head, block)
        a.local_count -= CACHE_SIZE/2
        unlock(a.global_lock)
```

## Correctness
- **No double-frees**: Each block has single owner at any time
- **No memory leaks**: All freed blocks eventually return to global pool
- **Bounds checking**: Fixed 64-byte blocks eliminate size tracking overhead
- **Thread safety**: Local caches provide thread isolation; global pool synchronized

## Fragmentation
- **Internal fragmentation**: Zero (fixed 64-byte blocks)
- **External fragmentation**: Minimal, since all blocks are identical size and fully managed via free lists
- **Local cache retention**: Blocks may sit idle in thread caches temporarily, but this is bounded and acceptable

## Worst-Case Latency
- **allocate()**: O(CACHE_SIZE) when local cache is empty and global pool must be drained; bounded by cache refill batch size
- **free()**: O(1) amortized; O(CACHE_SIZE) only when local cache drains to global pool
- **Contention**: Reduced significantly by per-thread caches; global lock held only during batch transfers

## Why This Is Asked
Tests mastery of crash‑mode semantics, NVM tooling, and low‑level synchronization. It probes data layout decisions, fence ordering, and recovery guarantees under power loss.

## Key Concepts
- Crash‑consistent queues on NVM
- Per‑slot sequence counters and ABA avoidance
- Fence/flush ordering and cache‑line alignment
- Recovery protocol after crash and in-flight slots
- Single‑producer, multi‑consumer design trade‑offs

## Code Example
```cpp
// Pseudo-code (high level)
struct Slot { uint64_t seq; char payload[P]; };
Slot *ring; size_t head, tail, N;
void enqueue(void* d){ auto t=tail; write_payload(&ring[t], d); ring[t].seq = t; mfence(); tail = t+1; }
void* dequeue(){ auto h=head; auto s = ring[h].seq; if(s==h){ auto d = read_payload(&ring[h]); ring[h].seq = h+1; mfence(); head = h+1; return d; } return NULL; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you support multiple producers safely?
- How would you quantify recovery time and data loss under abrupt power loss?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests lock-free IPC, memory ordering, and cache-coherence handling on NUMA systems under contention.

## Key Concepts
- Lock-free ring buffers with per-slot sequence numbers to avoid ABA
- Memory ordering on x86-64, mfence usage, cache-line padding
- Backpressure handling and wrap-around semantics

## Code Example
```c
typedef struct { volatile uint64_t seq; uint8_t data[64]; char pad[56]; } Slot;
typedef struct { Slot slots[N]; _Atomic uint64_t head; _Atomic uint64_t tail; } Ring;
```

```c
// Push (producer)
uint64_t pos; do { pos = atomic_read(&ring->head); if (slot_full(pos)) continue; } while(!atomic_compare_exchange(&ring->head, pos, pos+1));
r ing->slots[pos & (N-1)].data = payload; ring->slots[pos & (N-1)].seq = pos; mfence();
```

## Follow-up Questions

## Why This Is Asked
Tests fundamentals of low-level synchronization, memory ordering, and cache performance with a simple, fair mechanism that beginners can implement and reason about.

## Key Concepts
- Atomic operations and memory_order semantics
- Fairness via ticketing
- False sharing and cache-line padding
- Simple microbenchmarks to compare contention behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
// Pseudo-C: structure and lock/unlock in C with atomics
#include <stdatomic.h>
typedef struct { alignas(64) atomic_uint64_t next_ticket; atomic_uint64_t now_serving; } ticket_lock_t;
void lock(ticket_lock_t *l){ uint64_t t = atomic_fetch_add(&l->next_ticket,1); while (atomic_load(&l->now_serving) != t) {} }
void unlock(ticket_lock_t *l){ atomic_fetch_add(&l->now_serving,1); }
```
